blocks.text: **The task.** An array of heights represents vertical lines on a flat surface. Pick two lines so that the container they form with the surface holds the most water. Return that maximum area.

blocks.code:
input:   [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]
output:  49    (lines at index 1 and 8: height 7, width 7)

blocks.text: Water is limited by the **shorter** of the two lines — it spills over the lower one. So:
The brute force tries all pairs at O(N²). Two pointers does it in one pass, but the reasoning is subtler than the sorted case — the array is **not** sorted here.
Why moving the shorter line is correct
Start wide, at both ends: that is the maximum possible width. Any move inward loses width, so it can only pay off by gaining height.

Now suppose the left line is shorter. What if we moved the **taller** right line inward instead? Width shrinks by one, and the height is still capped by that same short left line — it cannot improve. Every such pair is worse than what we already have.
So the taller line can be dismissed as a mover. The only move with any chance is the **shorter** one — it is the binding constraint, and replacing it is the only way height can grow.
Most two pointer problems lean on sortedness. This one does not — the movement rule comes from an argument about which candidates can be safely discarded.
That is the general form of the pattern. Sortedness is just the most common reason such an argument exists, not the only one.
